lead: This unit teaches the two systematic ways to solve a circuit — mesh currents and node voltages — and the network theorems that replace a complicated circuit by a simple equivalent. After it you can solve DC circuits with independent and dependent sources, find Thevenin and Norton equivalents, choose a load for maximum power, and apply the same theorems to AC circuits using phasors.
about: Unit 2 turns Kirchhoff's laws into working methods. Chapter 2.1 writes KVL around mesh currents and handles current sources with a supermesh. Chapter 2.2 writes KCL at node voltages and handles voltage sources with a supernode. Chapter 2.3 proves that a linear circuit obeys superposition, so each source can be solved alone. Chapter 2.4 replaces any two-terminal network by a Thevenin or Norton equivalent. Chapter 2.5 chooses the load for maximum power. Chapter 2.6 adds reciprocity, Millman's and Tellegen's theorems as extra tools and checks. Chapter 2.7 repeats the theorems in the phasor domain with complex impedance, ending with conjugate matching.

chapters.idea: Mesh currents turn KVL around every loop into a small set of linear equations, and a shared current source becomes one supermesh equation plus one current constraint.
chapters.depth: Define a mesh as a loop that contains no other loop. Write KVL for each mesh in terms of mesh currents and set up the resistance matrix. Cover circuits with independent and dependent sources. For a current source shared by two meshes, remove that branch, write one supermesh KVL equation, and add the current constraint. Some syllabi call mesh analysis loop analysis. State that the method needs a planar circuit.
chapters.example: A two-mesh circuit has a 12 V source in the left mesh, a 2 Ω resistor in the top branch of the left mesh, a 5 A source pointing down in the shared branch, and a 4 Ω resistor in the right mesh. Find i₁ and i₂. The supermesh gives 2i₁ + 4i₂ = 12; the shared source gives i₁ − i₂ = 5. Solving: i₁ = 16/3 A = 5.333 A, i₂ = 1/3 A = 0.333 A.
chapters.trap: Using KVL through the ideal current source, or writing i₁ + i₂ = 5 instead of i₁ − i₂ = 5 for the shared branch.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: KVL, KCL, resistors, independent and dependent sources.
chapters.leave: AC mesh equations with phasors go to 2.7; full graph-theoretic mesh matrices go to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Node voltages turn KCL at every non-reference node into a small set of linear equations, and a voltage source between two nodes becomes one supernode equation plus one voltage constraint.
chapters.depth: Define node voltages relative to a reference node. Write KCL at each non-reference node; the coefficient matrix is a conductance matrix. Include dependent sources. For a voltage source between two non-reference nodes, form a supernode: write one KCL equation for the boundary and one voltage constraint. Some syllabi call this the node-voltage method. Show the matrix form for a circuit with three non-reference nodes.
chapters.example: In the circuit of the figure, find v₁ and v₂. The 5 V source sits between nodes 1 and 2, a 6 A source feeds node 2 from the reference, a 2 Ω resistor joins node 1 to reference, and a 3 Ω resistor joins node 2 to reference. Supernode KCL: v₁/2 + v₂/3 = 6. Constraint: v₁ − v₂ = 5. Solving: v₂ = 4.2 V, v₁ = 9.2 V.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that the voltage-source branch is left out of the supernode KCL, or reversing the constraint v₁ − v₂ = 5 V.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: KCL, node, branch, resistors, independent and dependent sources.
chapters.leave: AC nodal equations with phasors go to 2.7; graph-theoretic cut-set analysis goes to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: In a linear circuit the response to several sources is the sum of the responses to each independent source acting alone, with all other independent sources set to zero.
chapters.depth: State linearity as homogeneity and additivity. Superposition: keep one independent source, turn off the rest, solve, repeat for every source, then add. A voltage source off is a short; a current source off is an open. Dependent sources stay active. Show that power does not obey superposition because P = I²R is not linear. Include one circuit with a dependent source to show it is not switched off.
chapters.example: A 12 V source is in series with a 2 Ω resistor and feeds node A. A 6 Ω resistor and a 6 A current source from ground to A also connect node A to ground. Find V_A by superposition. With the 12 V source alone, V_A = 12 × 6/(2 + 6) = 9 V. With the 6 A source alone, V_A = 6 × (2 ∥ 6) = 6 × 1.5 = 9 V. Total V_A = 18 V.
chapters.trap: Superposing power (P = I²R is not linear) or switching off a dependent source.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: independent sources, series and parallel resistors; 2.1 and 2.2 for solving each reduced circuit.
chapters.leave: Superposition with different AC frequencies goes to 2.7; superposition in transient analysis goes to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced by a voltage source V_th in series with R_th, or by a current source I_N in parallel with R_N, where R_N = R_th and I_N = V_th/R_th.
chapters.depth: Define Thevenin voltage V_th as the open-circuit voltage and R_th as the resistance seen at the terminals with independent sources dead. Define Norton current I_N as the short-circuit current. Show the source transformation between the two forms. Explain the test-source method for R_th when dependent sources exist. Some syllabi call the pair Thevenin and Norton equivalents. Include one circuit with a dependent source only at the level of setting up the test source.
chapters.example: A 12 V source is in series with a 4 Ω resistor and feeds a 6 Ω resistor connected across the output terminals. Find the Thevenin equivalent. V_th = 12 × 6/(4 + 6) = 7.2 V. With the 12 V source shorted, R_th = 4 ∥ 6 = 2.4 Ω. The short-circuit current is I_sc = 12/4 = 3 A, and V_th/R_th = 7.2/2.4 = 3 A, so I_N = 3 A.
chapters.trap: Shorting a current source or opening a voltage source when finding R_th; forgetting the test source when a dependent source is present.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 and 2.2 to solve for V_oc and I_sc; Unit 1 source transformation.
chapters.leave: AC Thevenin and Norton with complex impedance go to 2.7; two-port equivalent parameters go to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A fixed Thevenin source delivers maximum power to a load when R_L = R_th, and that maximum is P_max = V_th²/(4R_th).
chapters.depth: Derive P_L = V_th² R_L/(R_th + R_L)². Set dP_L/dR_L = 0 to obtain R_L = R_th and P_max = V_th²/(4R_th). Show the power curve and its peak. Note that efficiency is only 50% at maximum power, so maximum power is not maximum efficiency. State the AC conjugate-match result and leave its proof to 2.7.
chapters.example: A Thevenin source has V_th = 12 V and R_th = 4 Ω. Find the load resistance for maximum power and the maximum power. R_L = R_th = 4 Ω. P_max = V_th²/(4R_th) = 12²/(4 × 4) = 144/16 = 9 W.
chapters.trap: Saying maximum power occurs at maximum efficiency, or applying R_L = R_th when R_th is not fixed.
chapters.leave: AC conjugate matching and P_max = |V_th|²/(4R_th) go to 2.7.

chapters.idea: Reciprocity swaps a source and a response in a linear bilateral network, Millman reduces parallel branches to one source, and Tellegen's theorem states that the sum of v_k i_k over all elements is zero.
chapters.depth: Reciprocity: in a linear bilateral network, moving an ideal source to the branch where the response was measured gives the same ratio of response to source. Millman: parallel branches with series voltage sources collapse to V = Σ(V_k/R_k)/Σ(1/R_k), with source polarities respected. Tellegen: for any network satisfying KCL and KVL, Σ v_k i_k = 0 with the passive sign convention. Some syllabi include Tellegen only as a statement; only a few universities ask for its proof.
chapters.example: Three parallel branches join nodes A and B. Branch 1: 10 V source in series with 2 Ω. Branch 2: 4 V source in series with 1 Ω. Branch 3: 0 V source in series with 4 Ω. All source positives face A. Find V_AB and the branch currents. V_AB = (10/2 + 4/1 + 0/4)/(1/2 + 1/1 + 1/4) = 9/1.75 = 5.143 V. Currents: (10 − 5.143)/2 = 2.429 A, (4 − 5.143)/1 = −1.143 A, (0 − 5.143)/4 = −1.286 A; their sum is zero.
chapters.trap: Ignoring source polarity in Millman's formula; applying reciprocity to a network with a dependent source; dropping the passive sign convention in Tellegen's sum.
chapters.prereq: 2.2 nodal analysis; 2.4 source transformation for Millman's formula.
chapters.leave: Full Tellegen proof using graph incidence matrices goes to Unit 1 network topology.

chapters.idea: Every network theorem holds in the phasor domain with complex impedance: Thevenin and Norton give V_th and Z_th, superposition works per frequency, and maximum power needs the conjugate match Z_L = Z_th*.
chapters.depth: Replace R by Z = R + jX and DC sources by phasors. Superposition: solve each frequency separately, then add time-domain waveforms, not phasors of different frequencies. Thevenin/Norton: find V_th and Z_th with independent sources dead. Maximum power: Z_L = Z_th* gives P_max = |V_th|²/(4R_th) with V_th in RMS; R_th is the real part of Z_th. Include one numerical example with a complex divider.
chapters.example: An AC source V_s = 10∠0° V RMS feeds a series impedance Z₁ = 2 + j2 Ω, and a shunt impedance Z₂ = 2 − j2 Ω is connected across the output. Find V_th, Z_th, the load for maximum power, and P_max. V_th = 10 × (2 − j2)/(2 + j2 + 2 − j2) = 10 × (2 − j2)/4 = 5 − j5 V = 7.071∠−45° V. Z_th = Z₁ ∥ Z₂ = 2 Ω. For maximum power, Z_L = Z_th* = 2 Ω. P_max = |V_th|²/(4R_th) = 50/(4 × 2) = 6.25 W.
chapters.trap: Using Z_L = R_th instead of the conjugate Z_th*, or adding phasors from sources of different frequencies.
chapters.prereq: 2.4 and 2.5; Unit 3 phasors, impedance and admittance.
chapters.leave: Three-phase power and the two-wattmeter method go to Unit 3; resonance and Q factor go to Unit 4.

links: mesh currents and node voltages are companion methods for the same circuit
nodal analysis gives the open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current
linearity is the reason a whole network can be replaced by one source and one resistance
mesh analysis solves each source-alone circuit in superposition
maximum power uses the Thevenin resistance and voltage
the Thevenin equivalent carries over with complex impedance
DC R_L = R_th becomes conjugate matching in AC
Millman's theorem is a one-step nodal solution for parallel branches
